about.subtitle: SlopeWorks is Carmen ter Heide and Bas Lazaroms. We organise complete company ski trips in Austria and Switzerland, not from a catalogue, but by visiting every area ourselves. In the end it isn't about how many areas we know, but about knowing which area fits which team.
about.story.label: Our story
about.story.title: How SlopeWorks began
about.story.p1: Carmen and Bas will happily talk about skiing the moment the temperature dips below 20 degrees. Which is fairly often. A friend of ours heard it often enough and at some point said: “If you love skiing this much, why don't you organise ski trips for companies?” Good question, really. That's how SlopeWorks began.
about.story.p2: Today we organise complete ski trips for companies in Austria and Switzerland. And the more we do it, the clearer one thing becomes: a good company ski trip doesn't start with the ski area, but with the people going along. That's why we first want to know who you are. Who can ski? Who never has? Who's at the first lift at half past eight, and who values a long lunch just as much? Do you mainly want a great time, or should the trip also do something for the team?
about.story.p3: Then we work out which destination fits and arrange the rest: from transport and hotel to lift passes, equipment, lessons, restaurants, activities and communication with the participants. And during the trip, we're there in person. Because however much we enjoy talking about skiing, in the end the person who got the trip going internally should above all be able to enjoy it themselves.

solden.intro1: Sölden isn't a resort we'd recommend to just any company by default.
solden.intro2: But if you have an active group, plenty of strong skiers and colleagues who aren't ready for bed after the last run down? Then it's a different story.
solden.sec.1.title: Why Sölden?
solden.sec.1.body: Sölden is quite emphatically about skiing. The area is high, sporty and, thanks to its glaciers, snow-sure, and the village has a lively après-ski scene. That makes Sölden especially strong for teams who genuinely want to spend a lot of time on the mountain during a company ski trip.
solden.sec.2.title: Skiing with experienced, keen skiers
solden.sec.2.body: This is where Sölden comes into its own. There's plenty of terrain for several solid ski days, and experienced skiers find more challenge here than in a destination aimed mainly at beginners. That doesn't mean beginners can't join. We can simply arrange lessons. But if 70% of your group has never skied, we wouldn't start with how to get everyone onto Sölden's slopes; we'd first look at whether Sölden is the best choice at all.
solden.sec.3.title: How snow-sure is Sölden?
solden.sec.3.body: The altitude and two glaciers make snow reliability a key advantage of Sölden. That also keeps the area interesting when you want to travel relatively early or later in the season. For every request we always look at the specific period and current conditions before proposing anything.
solden.sec.4.title: Skiing on the glaciers
solden.sec.4.body: The glaciers give Sölden not only extra snow reliability but also a different kind of ski day. For groups who come purely to ski, that's one of the reasons we might rank Sölden above a more general destination.
solden.sec.5.title: Is Sölden suitable if not everyone skis?
solden.sec.5.body: It can be, but this isn't where Sölden scores its highest marks with us. A few non-skiers we can easily fit into the programme. If a large part of the group doesn't ski, we find Mayrhofen, Zell am See-Kaprun or Gstaad more interesting to explore.
solden.sec.6.title: Après-ski with colleagues
solden.sec.6.body: Sölden is lively after skiing. For some teams that's exactly the point; for others not at all. That's why we simply ask during the intake. If no one in your company is looking for après-ski, there's little sense in picking a destination that's known precisely for it.
solden.sec.7.title: Hotels for company groups
solden.sec.7.body: Sölden is a long, stretched-out village. As a result, the hotel's location can have a considerable impact on the logistics of the trip. We look at access to the lifts, group size, desired level of comfort, the evening programme and budget before proposing a hotel.
solden.sec.8.title: Getting to Sölden
solden.sec.8.body: Sölden can be reached by coach, plane or car. Flying via Innsbruck can be attractive, but for a larger group a coach from the Netherlands or Belgium is often more practical. We sort this out and can organise the transport entirely.
solden.sec.9.title: What's the best time to go?
solden.sec.9.body: Thanks to its altitude and glaciers, Sölden has a relatively long season. Which week is most interesting, however, also depends on how busy it is, availability and budget. That's why we always look at the period and the hotel together.
solden.sec.10.title: What does a company ski trip to Sölden cost?
solden.sec.10.body: On price, Sölden sits above our most accessible destinations. But the final figure depends far more on your choices than on the village alone. During the intake we therefore discuss the budget, so we can then look specifically for a trip that genuinely fits within it.

faq.title: FAQ about your corporate ski trip.
faq.subtitle: Before you book a call, here are the answers to the questions HR and office managers ask us most.
faq.werk.title: How it works
faq.werk.sub: What sets SlopeWorks apart from a travel agency or booking portal.
faq.werk.q1: What makes SlopeWorks different from a travel agency or a corporate-wintersport specialist?
faq.werk.a1: We don't book from a fixed catalogue. We work with a limited number of groups per season, in areas we've been to ourselves, with hotel owners we know by name. No fixed programme that's the same for every group, a proposal that starts with a conversation about your team.
faq.werk.q2: What does the process look like from first contact?
faq.werk.a2: You tell us what you're looking for: group size, dates, budget, and what kind of team it is. Then we put together one proposal, not three packages to choose between. Once agreed, we arrange accommodation, transport, ski pass and programme, with one point of contact through to the last day.
faq.werk.q3: Do you also work with a team coach or facilitator?
faq.werk.a3: For teams that want it, we work with Kamp Vuur. It's not a bolt-on we add to every trip, but something we factor into how we build the programme, based on what the team needs.
faq.werk.q4: Do you also handle communication with participants?
faq.werk.a4: Yes. It's one of the things we take off the internal organiser's plate. We answer participants' practical questions, so it doesn't all land on that one colleague.
faq.prijs.title: Pricing and budget
faq.prijs.sub: What a corporate ski trip costs on average and how we build up prices.
faq.prijs.q1: What does a corporate ski trip cost on average per person?
faq.prijs.a1: That depends on destination, duration and programme. We don't work with fixed entry prices you have to top up later. Based on what your team needs, we put together one complete proposal, including accommodation, ski pass, local transport and dinners.
faq.prijs.q2: Are there hidden costs in a SlopeWorks proposal?
faq.prijs.a2: No. The proposal you receive is the amount you pay. What's included is fixed in advance, so you can defend it internally without surprises afterwards.
faq.prijs.q3: Can I request a quote with no obligation?
faq.prijs.a3: Yes. The first conversation is without obligation. We want to know what your team needs before we propose anything, not the other way around.
faq.groep.title: Groups and level
faq.groep.sub: Who a SlopeWorks trip suits, and who it doesn't.
faq.groep.q1: What group size does SlopeWorks organise trips for?
faq.groep.a1: We organise trips for groups of up to 50 people. At that group size we can keep building a tailored programme without it becoming a large, impersonal coach trip.
faq.groep.q2: Is a SlopeWorks trip suitable if not everyone can ski?
faq.groep.a2: Yes, in most areas we build a dedicated programme for non-skiers, so nobody spends a day alone at the hotel. Some destinations, like Sölden, do lean more toward teams that mostly already have skiing experience.
faq.groep.q3: Can a group with mixed levels still travel together?
faq.groep.a3: Yes. We build the programme by level, from first time on skis to experienced skier, so nobody has to wait for anyone and the group still ends the day together.
faq.best.title: Destinations
faq.best.sub: Which areas we offer and how to choose.
faq.best.q1: Which countries does SlopeWorks organise ski trips in?
faq.best.a1: We're active in Austria and Switzerland. France is planned for next year, but for now we deliberately choose quality over quantity and only work with areas we know well ourselves.
faq.best.q2: Which ski area suits our team best?
faq.best.a2: That depends on the group's level, the budget and what you want to experience. Have a look at the destinations page for an overview, or tell us about your team and we'll think along.
faq.best.q3: What's the difference between the areas SlopeWorks offers?
faq.best.a3: Sölden is sporty and glacier-sure, Mayrhofen is energetic with room for non-skiers, St. Anton has a serious reputation for its pistes, Kitzbühel is well-known and polished, Zell am See is quieter than it looks on paper, and Gstaad sits a tier above the rest in price and refinement.
faq.prakt.title: Practical matters
faq.prakt.sub: Planning, timing and what we need from you.
faq.prakt.q1: When should we book for the ski season?
faq.prakt.a1: The earlier the better for choice of accommodation and dates. For the busier high-season weeks we recommend planning at least four to six months ahead.
faq.prakt.q2: Does SlopeWorks also arrange transport to the ski area?
faq.prakt.a2: Yes. Depending on the group, coach, flight, car or a combination of these can be part of the proposal, including the local transfers. That way you don't have to separately sort out a coach company or flights internally.
faq.prakt.q3: What happens if someone drops out at the last minute?
faq.prakt.a3: We discuss that upfront in the cancellation terms, so there's no ambiguity if it happens. Where possible we build in flexibility so a single drop-out doesn't immediately add costs for the group.
faq.prakt.q4: Does SlopeWorks come along on the trip itself?
faq.prakt.a4: Yes. We guide the group on location too. A run sheet is useful until a flight changes, someone's missing equipment or the weather doesn't cooperate. That's when you want someone there to sort it out.

comparison.title: SlopeWorks compared to an ordinary travel agency.
comparison.subtitle: There are roughly two kinds of provider you meet when looking for a corporate ski trip. Here we explain how SlopeWorks relates to them, without a sales pitch.
comparison.runs.label: The three routes
comparison.runs.title: Three ways down the same mountain
comparison.runs.lead: One mountain, three lines down. Which route suits you depends on your team, your budget and how hands-on you want to be, not on which is 'best'.
comparison.deep.label: The long read
comparison.glance.type.g: Broad tour operator, also sun and family holidays
comparison.glance.strength.u: Knowledge of the area from first-hand experience
comparison.dd1.title: Why people look for an alternative
comparison.dd1.p1: Most companies organising a ski trip run into the same problem. Someone has to do it on top of their own job, and booking a package is quickly done, but it often feels like a standard trip with a different logo on it. The organiser mostly hears afterwards about the things that weren't quite right: the hotel that was further from the lift than expected, the restaurant that couldn't handle a group of twenty.
comparison.dd1.p2: That's no reproach to the existing providers. Both types do what they promise, at scale and with plenty of experience. It's a different choice: scale and convenience, or a smaller, personal approach.
comparison.dd2.title: The generalist: sharp prices, broad offering
comparison.dd2.p1: Some providers are first and foremost a holiday tour operator. Wintersport group trips are then one part of a broader offering that also includes sun holidays and family trips. With hundreds of destinations and a strong negotiating position with ski areas, the strength lies in price and choice, not in specialisation in corporate trips.
comparison.dd2.p2: For a company mostly watching its budget, with little need for a tailored programme, that's a logical choice. For a team looking for an experience that fits their own culture, such a generalist package offers little to hold on to.
comparison.dd3.title: The specialist: a strong, repeatable operation
comparison.dd3.p1: Other providers have devoted themselves entirely to corporate wintersport, at a scale that commands respect: hundreds of companies and thousands of participants a year, often with well-known names as clients. A booking portal and app keep the process tightly organised, and every group gets a fixed contact.
comparison.dd3.p2: That scale has another side. This kind of provider works with a select number of fixed destinations and a programme tuned per sector, but always within a fixed structure. A strong choice for a company seeking a reliable, repeatable experience. For a team that wants something not every other client experiences that season too, it's less distinctive.
comparison.dd4.title: SlopeWorks: smaller, but from first-hand experience
comparison.dd4.p1: SlopeWorks deliberately chooses a different starting point. Rather than scaling to thousands of participants, we work with a limited number of groups per season. Every area we propose (Sölden, Mayrhofen, St. Anton, Kitzbühel, Zell am See or Gstaad) we've visited ourselves. We know the hotel owners by name and know which restaurant can serve a group of twenty without compromising on quality.
comparison.dd4.p2: That also means an honest limitation: we can't send a quote within 48 hours the way a large specialist can, and we're not the cheapest option. What we do offer is a programme built around a specific team, with knowledge that doesn't come from a catalogue.
comparison.who.g.title: Choose a generalist if
comparison.who.g.body: Budget is the most important factor, you want to book quickly without much coordination, and a standard programme works for the group.
comparison.who.s.title: Choose a specialist if
comparison.who.s.body: You have a large group, want a fully automated process via a booking portal, and a proven, repeatable approach matters more than bespoke work.
comparison.who.u.title: Choose SlopeWorks if
comparison.who.u.body: Your team is between 15 and 40 people, you want a programme that fits who you are, and you value a provider that knows the area itself rather than from a database.

gstaad.intro1: Gstaad is expensive. Let's just get that out of the way first.
gstaad.intro2: But for the right group, it can be exactly the destination you're looking for.
gstaad.sec.1.title: Why Gstaad for a company ski trip?
gstaad.sec.1.body: Gstaad is less about racking up as many piste kilometres as possible and more about the complete experience. Luxury, calm, service and image play a bigger role here. At the same time the area is accessible for beginners, and there are good options for colleagues who don't want to ski at all.
gstaad.sec.2.title: When is Gstaad worth its higher price?
gstaad.sec.2.body: When the group values luxury, service, calm, good restaurants and a trip that isn't all about skiing. Is everyone mainly keen to ski hard for three days and then dive straight into the après-ski? Then we probably wouldn't spend the extra money on Gstaad.
gstaad.sec.3.title: Skiing with beginners and advanced skiers in Gstaad
gstaad.sec.3.body: Gstaad is friendly to beginners. Experienced skiers have options too, but the character is different from the far more sporty St. Anton or Sölden. That makes it interesting for a group where the differences in ability are large.
gstaad.sec.4.title: What can non-skiers do in Gstaad?
gstaad.sec.4.body: Plenty. And that matters, because on a premium company trip in particular you don't want colleagues who don't ski to feel like second-rate participants. So we build a programme in which they can take part fully as well.
gstaad.sec.5.title: Gstaad or Saanenmöser: where do you stay with a company group?
gstaad.sec.5.body: You don't necessarily have to stay in the middle of Gstaad to make use of the region. Saanenmöser can be attractive for groups thanks to its location, hotels and access to the ski area. We actually prefer it: you're closer to the slopes and you're not stuck in traffic driving in and out of Gstaad every day. This is exactly the kind of choice where local knowledge can make a real difference.
gstaad.sec.6.title: Luxury, calm and activities off the slopes
gstaad.sec.6.body: Gstaad doesn't have to become a trip where everyone is locked into a tight programme from breakfast to dinner. The space and the higher level of service can be part of the experience in themselves. A long lunch can sometimes be a better choice here than yet another organised activity.
gstaad.sec.7.title: Hotels for company groups in Gstaad and Saanenmöser
gstaad.sec.7.body: At this destination the choice of hotel has an enormous impact on the budget. That's why we look at what you actually need. Luxury for its own sake makes little sense. Luxury because it fits the team and the purpose of the trip does.
gstaad.sec.8.title: Getting to Gstaad from the Netherlands
gstaad.sec.8.body: Flying via Geneva with a transfer is one option. Train, bus and car can also be worthwhile depending on the group. We include transport in the overall proposal.
gstaad.sec.9.title: What is the best time for a company ski trip to Gstaad?
gstaad.sec.9.body: We look at snow conditions, how busy it is, availability and price. Around popular holiday weeks and public holidays, both the atmosphere and the price level can change considerably.
gstaad.sec.10.title: What does a company ski trip to Gstaad cost?
gstaad.sec.10.body: More than our Austrian destinations. A large, luxury company trip can run up a serious bill here. That's why we ask about the budget early during the intake. Not because we want to know how much we can spend, but because there's no point designing a beautiful trip that then never gets past management or Finance.

gstaad.fit.yes3: A group of 50 is possible too, as long as you understand what that choice means financially.

gstaad.fit.no3: The group is mostly serious, hard-charging skiers. If image matters but Gstaad goes too far financially, Kitzbühel is often a smarter alternative.

mayrhofen.intro1: Mayrhofen is, as far as we're concerned, one of the easiest areas to recommend to a company where all kinds of people are mixed together.
mayrhofen.intro2: Strong skiers, beginners, colleagues who mainly come along for the fun, and people who don't want to ski at all: there's plenty of room to move here. And on a company ski trip that often matters more than the sheer number of piste kilometres.
mayrhofen.sec.1.title: Why Mayrhofen?
mayrhofen.sec.1.body: Mayrhofen is an all-rounder. You get good skiing, a lively village, well-known après-ski and plenty to do for colleagues who don't want to be on the slopes every day. On top of that, prices sit lower than at destinations like St. Anton and Gstaad. For a group with different wishes, that gives you relatively a lot of room to build a trip that works for everyone.
mayrhofen.sec.2.title: Skiing with beginners and experts alike
mayrhofen.sec.2.body: A company group doesn't need the same ski level to travel together. In Mayrhofen beginners can ease in with lessons while experienced skiers head out into the area. Penken and Ahorn offer plenty of options, and anyone after more of a challenge can go deeper into the Zillertal, up onto the glacier, or take on one of the most notorious valley descents in the world: the Eberharter Goldpiste. All of it within half an hour's drive.
mayrhofen.sec.3.title: What can non-skiers do?
mayrhofen.sec.3.body: Mayrhofen is actually a strong choice when not everyone wants to ski. There's a range of winter activities on offer, and the village itself is lively enough for a good day out even without ski boots. Hintertux, for example, is about half an hour's drive away. We don't decide the activities in advance: it depends on how many non-skiers come along and what they actually feel like doing.
mayrhofen.sec.4.title: Après-ski and activities with colleagues
mayrhofen.sec.4.body: If your team loves après-ski, Mayrhofen has you covered. But a company ski trip doesn't have to be three days of après-ski, of course. We can combine ski days with shared lunches, dinners and other activities. The real question is: what gets your group excited? That's what we build the programme around.
mayrhofen.sec.5.title: Hotels for company groups
mayrhofen.sec.5.body: With a hotel we look beyond price and star rating. Where does it sit relative to the lifts? Can we have breakfast there as a whole group? How easily can non-skiers get away? Does it match the level of comfort you want? And can we run the programme logically from there? For a group of 40, the best hotel can therefore be a different one than for a group of 12.
mayrhofen.sec.6.title: Getting to Mayrhofen
mayrhofen.sec.6.body: Mayrhofen is reachable by coach, train, plane and car. Which option works best depends on group size, departure point, travel time and budget. We can fold transport into the complete trip, so you don't end up separately sourcing a coach company, transfers or flights in-house.
mayrhofen.sec.7.title: When is the best time to go?
mayrhofen.sec.7.body: That depends on what matters to you. The timing affects snow conditions, crowds, hotel availability and price. That's why, during the intake, we ask not only where you want to go but also when you can travel. From there we look at what actually makes sense and is available at that moment.
mayrhofen.sec.8.title: What does a company ski trip cost?
mayrhofen.sec.8.body: There's no standard figure for that. A trip with 15 colleagues for a few days in a simpler hotel is a very different thing from an extensive programme for 50 people. The number of participants, transport, hotel, travel time, ski passes, equipment, lessons, food and activities all ultimately determine the price. Among our six destinations, Mayrhofen does sit on the more accessible end.

stanton.intro1: St. Anton needs little introduction among skiers. But that doesn't mean every company should automatically head there.
stanton.intro2: For a group with plenty of experienced skiers, St. Anton can be superb. For twenty beginners who mainly want a fun first ski trip together, there are more logical choices.
stanton.sec.1.title: Why St. Anton?
stanton.sec.1.body: Ski Arlberg is big, challenging and interesting for people who want to ski seriously. Add its reputation and famous après-ski, and you get a destination with a very clear character. That comes with a higher price tag too.
stanton.sec.2.title: How well does your team need to ski?
stanton.sec.2.body: Not everyone has to be an expert. But it gets more rewarding when enough strong skiers come along who will actually use the terrain. Beginners can take lessons, but for a group made up almost entirely of beginners, other areas are friendlier.
stanton.sec.3.title: Skiing Ski Arlberg with colleagues
stanton.sec.3.body: This is the main reason to choose St. Anton. The area offers plenty of kilometres and challenging terrain. That lets you have different groups ski at their own level and regroup at set moments later on.
stanton.sec.4.title: What can beginners do?
stanton.sec.4.body: We arrange lessons in advance. That way beginners don't have to trail after experienced colleagues, and the experienced skiers don't have to play instructor all trip. Nicer for everyone.
stanton.sec.5.title: Is St. Anton suitable for non-skiers?
stanton.sec.5.body: A few non-skiers we can happily bring along. But if a large part of your team doesn't ski, St. Anton wouldn't be our first choice. There's little point spending a lot of money on a destination whose greatest strength much of the group barely uses.
stanton.sec.6.title: Après-ski in St. Anton
stanton.sec.6.body: Après-ski is part of St. Anton's character. For a group that's up for it, that's a plus. Does your team mainly want good food, calm and luxury without much partying? Then we'd also look at Kitzbühel or Gstaad.
stanton.sec.7.title: Hotels for company groups
stanton.sec.7.body: Location can cost a lot of money here. A hotel right by the lift can be considerably more expensive than a good option a little further out. With smart transport, that second option can sometimes make far more sense for a company group.
stanton.sec.8.title: Why is St. Anton more expensive?
stanton.sec.8.body: Popularity, accommodation and location all play a part. Here you pay for a destination with a strong name and a large, high-quality ski area. So the relevant question isn't only: "Can we afford St. Anton?" But also: "Will our group use what we're paying for?"
stanton.sec.9.title: Getting to St. Anton
stanton.sec.9.body: We can include coach, flights, transfers and other transport options in the proposal. Which route makes sense depends on group size, departure point, budget and desired travel time.
stanton.sec.10.title: When's the best time to go?
stanton.sec.10.body: Popular weeks can be busy and pricey. Booking early gives more choice, especially when you need enough rooms in the same hotel for a larger group.
stanton.sec.11.title: What does a company ski trip cost?
stanton.sec.11.body: St. Anton sits at the higher end of our Austrian range. We can only give an exact price once we know group size, dates, hotel level, transport and programme.

kitzbuhel.intro1: Kitzbühel has the reputation. Kirchberg has a character all its own.
kitzbuhel.intro2: And it is exactly that combination that makes the area interesting for a company group.
kitzbuhel.sec.1.title: Why Kitzbühel-Kirchberg for a company ski trip?
kitzbuhel.sec.1.body: You get a large ski area that is accessible to a range of levels, combined with a choice between the style of Kitzbühel and the buzz of Kirchberg. For mixed teams with a little more budget, that is an interesting combination.
kitzbuhel.sec.2.title: Kitzbühel or Kirchberg: where does your company want to stay?
kitzbuhel.sec.2.body: That depends on the group. Kitzbühel is more stylish and generally more expensive. Kirchberg is livelier and can be more appealing when après-ski matters. You can use the same ski area and still get a fairly different company trip depending on where you stay.
kitzbuhel.sec.3.title: Skiing with beginners and advanced skiers in Kitzbühel
kitzbuhel.sec.3.body: The area has plenty of accessible runs for beginners and enough terrain for experienced skiers. And yes, for the die-hards there is of course the Streif. Not everyone has to ski it. In fact, for some of your colleagues skipping it is probably an excellent idea.
kitzbuhel.sec.4.title: Is Kitzbühel suitable for colleagues who don't ski?
kitzbuhel.sec.4.body: Yes. The village and the surrounding area offer plenty to do so that non-skiers stay part of the trip too. With a high percentage of non-skiers, we would shape the programme around that from the start.
kitzbuhel.sec.5.title: Après-ski in Kitzbühel and Kirchberg
kitzbuhel.sec.5.body: If you want a lot of après-ski, we look firmly at Kirchberg. If you want more style, restaurants and calm instead, Kitzbühel may be the better fit. This is exactly why “we want to go to Kitzbühel” is not yet enough information for us.
kitzbuhel.sec.6.title: Luxury and prestige without going to Gstaad
kitzbuhel.sec.6.body: Kitzbühel can be an interesting choice when the team values style and quality, but Gstaad is a step too far in price or character. Here you get luxury without the whole trip automatically taking on Gstaad's price level.
kitzbuhel.sec.7.title: Hotels for company groups in Kitzbühel-Kirchberg
kitzbuhel.sec.7.body: The hotel choice is closely tied to the choice between the two towns. We look at group size, budget, location, luxury and the evening programme you want.
kitzbuhel.sec.8.title: Getting to Kitzbühel-Kirchberg
kitzbuhel.sec.8.body: Coach, train, plane or car are all options. We compare what makes sense for your group and can arrange the entire journey.
kitzbuhel.sec.9.title: What is the best time for a company ski trip to Kitzbühel?
kitzbuhel.sec.9.body: We determine that based on snow, crowds, availability and price. With larger groups, starting early matters especially, because you are not looking for one room but sometimes twenty or more.
kitzbuhel.sec.10.title: What does a company ski trip to Kitzbühel-Kirchberg cost?
kitzbuhel.sec.10.body: That depends, among other things, on where you stay. Kitzbühel itself can turn out considerably more expensive than alternatives nearby. During the intake we therefore first work out how much value you place on luxury and location.

kitzbuhel.fit.yes2: Style and a good hotel matter to you.
kitzbuhel.fit.yes3: You want a strong middle ground: less overtly sporty than St. Anton, less extremely luxurious than Gstaad.

zellamsee.intro1: One person wants to ski for three days. Another wants to try it once. And a third has already said they won't be putting on ski boots at all.
zellamsee.intro2: For a team like that, Zell am See-Kaprun gets interesting.
zellamsee.sec.1.title: Why Zell am See-Kaprun for a company ski trip?
zellamsee.sec.1.body: Its strength is flexibility. You have Zell am See, the Schmittenhöhe, Kaprun and the Kitzsteinhorn in the same region. That lets us build different kinds of days without the group feeling like everyone is on a separate holiday.
zellamsee.sec.2.title: Why Zell am See-Kaprun works for a mixed group
zellamsee.sec.2.body: A company trip is not only about the best skiers. If ten colleagues have a great time and the other twenty are mainly waiting for dinner to start, we have planned the wrong trip. In Zell am See-Kaprun we have more room to let different needs sit side by side.
zellamsee.sec.3.title: Skiing on the Schmittenhöhe and Kitzsteinhorn
zellamsee.sec.3.body: The Schmittenhöhe sits right next to Zell am See. On top of that, the Kitzsteinhorn near Kaprun offers high-altitude winter-sport terrain. That combination gives us more options depending on skiing level, weather and time of year.
zellamsee.sec.4.title: Skiing with beginners and advanced skiers
zellamsee.sec.4.body: Beginners can take lessons and experienced skiers can cover more terrain on their own. We plan shared moments, but nobody has to ski at the wrong level for three days just because "we're here with the company."
zellamsee.sec.5.title: What can non-skiers do in Zell am See-Kaprun?
zellamsee.sec.5.body: This is actually one of the reasons to choose the destination. The lake, Zell am See itself and the wider region offer plenty to do off the slopes. That lets us build a full alternative programme.
zellamsee.sec.6.title: Zell am See or Kaprun: where is it best to stay?
zellamsee.sec.6.body: That depends on your programme. Zell am See gives you the character of the lake and a livelier town. Kaprun can be more interesting for logistics and for certain group activities. So we don't automatically go for the best-known name.
zellamsee.sec.7.title: Activities with colleagues off the slopes
zellamsee.sec.7.body: Not everything has to be labelled a team-building activity. We prefer to look at things people genuinely enjoy, where colleagues naturally end up spending time with someone new. That can achieve far more than a forced exercise in a hotel meeting room.
zellamsee.sec.8.title: Hotels and restaurants for company groups
zellamsee.sec.8.body: With a large group the choices change. A lovely restaurant for four can be completely unworkable for 40 colleagues. So we look at capacity and logistics in advance and factor restaurants into the planning.
zellamsee.sec.9.title: Getting to Zell am See-Kaprun
zellamsee.sec.9.body: Depending on your group we arrange coach, plane, car or a combination. We also handle local transport where it is needed.
zellamsee.sec.10.title: When is the best time for a company ski trip to Zell am See?
zellamsee.sec.10.body: That depends on crowds, availability, budget and snow conditions. The Kitzsteinhorn adds extra options thanks to its altitude.
zellamsee.sec.11.title: What does a company ski trip to Zell am See-Kaprun cost?
zellamsee.sec.11.body: Zell am See-Kaprun sits at the more accessible end of our range, but there is no fixed price. After the intake we put together a proposal based on your actual group and wishes.

home.team.label: Our approach
home.team.title: The team first. The destination second.
home.team.body1: Most ski trips start with: "We want to go to Sölden." We'd rather start with: "Who's actually coming along?" Are they keen skiers, or is half the group on skis for the first time? Does everyone want to be at the first lift by 08:30, or is a long lunch just as important? What do the non-skiers do? Do you mainly want to celebrate something, or should the trip also help colleagues get to know each other better? And how much comfort suits the group and the budget?
home.team.body2: Only once we know all that do we look at the destination. Sometimes that's Sölden. Sometimes Mayrhofen. And sometimes the area no one had in mind turns out to be a much better fit. The team first. The destination second.
home.services.label: What we handle
home.services.title: The whole ski trip, already handled
home.services.intro: From transport to on-location support: we take the entire trip off your hands, so you can simply be there.
home.services.s1.title: Transport
home.services.s1.body: Coach, plane, own transport or a combination. We look at what's practical for your group and include it in the proposal.
home.services.s2.title: Hotel
home.services.s2.body: Not just any hotel with enough rooms. We consider location, group size, ability level, the comfort you want, the evening programme and what's happening around the hotel.
home.services.s3.title: Passes, rental & lessons
home.services.s3.body: Arranged in advance, so the first morning doesn't start with 35 colleagues queuing at the rental shop.
home.services.s4.title: Restaurants
home.services.s4.body: A restaurant that's cosy for four isn't automatically right for forty. We look for places that suit the group and the programme. And that serve genuinely good food, of course.
home.services.s5.title: Activities for everyone
home.services.s5.body: Not everyone has to ski three days straight to be part of the trip. There's plenty to do for people who have never been on skis and have no wish to start.
home.services.s6.title: Participant communication
home.services.s6.body: We answer participants' practical questions, so it doesn't all land on that one colleague.
home.services.s7.title: Support on location
home.services.s7.body: Once the trip begins, we don't disappear. We come along. Because a plan is useful, right up until a flight changes, someone is missing equipment, an activity overruns or the weather decides not to cooperate. That's when you want someone there to fix it.
home.outcome.label: The goal
home.outcome.title: What should your company ski trip deliver?
home.outcome.intro: Not every company trip needs to become a cultural programme. Sometimes a team has simply earned it. That's fine. But if you're spending tens of thousands of euros sending colleagues into the mountains together, it's worth asking one question up front: what do we want this trip to deliver?
home.outcome.reward.title: Reward
home.outcome.reward.body: We've worked hard and we've earned this. The focus is on skiing, fun, good food and sharing something special together.
home.outcome.together.title: Better Together
home.outcome.together.body: The trip can be great fun and help colleagues get to know each other in a different way. No compulsory trust exercises. Just moments and activities that naturally bring people together with colleagues they don't usually work with.
home.outcome.reset.title: Reset
home.outcome.reset.body: Something is going on within the team and the trip can help get things moving again. In that case our intake goes beyond ski experience and hotel preferences.
home.destinations.card4.tagline: The stylish all-rounder. Beginners and advanced skiers both feel at home here. Kitzbühel brings the flair, Kirchberg brings the energy.
home.destinations.card5.tagline: The serious skier. A destination for groups who ski well, look for a challenge and are willing to spend a little more for it.
home.destinations.card6.tagline: The luxury choice. Calm, Switzerland, good options for beginners and non-skiers and a price level clearly above the other five destinations.
home.process.label: How it works
home.process.title: How we organise your company ski trip
home.process.step1.title: 30 minutes about your team
home.process.step1.body: No hours-long briefing. In 30 minutes at most, we want to understand who's coming along, what matters to you and what the trip needs to deliver.
home.process.step2.title: We start searching
home.process.step2.body: Then we look into which destination fits, which hotels are available and what's possible for your dates. Give us roughly 2 to 3 working days for that.
home.process.step3.title: You receive a proposal
home.process.step3.body: Not a standard package that happens to still be free. A proposal built around your group, your wishes and your budget.
home.process.step4.title: We arrange the trip
home.process.step4.body: Once you approve, we get to work on transport, accommodation, lift passes, equipment, lessons, food, activities and participant communication.
home.process.step5.title: We come along
home.process.step5.body: We're there in person during the trip. So you don't have to make one colleague responsible after all for everything that happens on location.
home.faq.label: Frequently asked questions
home.faq.title: Frequently asked questions about a company ski trip
home.faq.q1: What does a company ski trip cost?
home.faq.a1: That depends heavily on the destination, the number of participants, the length of the trip, transport, accommodation and programme. That's why we don't work with a single standard price per person. After the intake, we look into what suits your group and budget and put together a complete proposal.
home.faq.q2: For how many people does SlopeWorks organise company ski trips?
home.faq.a2: We organise trips for groups of up to 50 participants. Which destination works best also depends on the size of the group.
home.faq.q3: Does everyone have to be able to ski?
home.faq.a3: No. That's exactly why we look at the make-up of the group in advance. We can arrange lessons for beginners and build in alternatives for non-skiers. Some destinations are far better suited to this than others.
home.faq.q4: Do you arrange transport as well?
home.faq.a4: Yes. Depending on the group, coach, plane, car or a combination of these can be part of the proposal.
home.faq.q5: Do you handle communication with participants too?
home.faq.a5: Yes. That's actually one of the ways we take the load off the internal organiser.
home.faq.q6: Does SlopeWorks come along on the trip?
home.faq.a6: Yes. We guide the group on location as well.
home.faq.q7: When should we book a company ski trip?
home.faq.a7: The sooner your dates and group size are known, the more choice you'll have in hotels and options. For popular weeks in particular, availability can narrow quickly. So our advice is to start well in advance, especially since internal budgets and approvals are often involved too.
home.faq.q8: Do you only organise trips to Austria?
home.faq.a8: No. We currently work in Austria and Switzerland. France is planned for next year, but for now we're choosing quality over quantity. So only areas we've visited several times ourselves and tested thoroughly.
howitworks.titleLead: Organise a company ski trip without having to
howitworks.sub: Organise a company ski trip without all the legwork. You tell us who's coming and what matters to you; we put the trip together and arrange everything from transport to on-site support.
howitworks.intro1: Organising a ski trip with colleagues often starts with plenty of enthusiasm. Until you start comparing hotels, working out who can ski, requesting transport quotes, dividing up rooms, finding restaurants for 30 people, and everyone suddenly turns out to have their own individual questions.
howitworks.intro2: That's why we take the bulk of that work off your hands. You tell us who's coming and what matters to you. We then work out which trip fits and arrange it. Here's how that works.
howitworks.step1.title: 30 minutes about your team
howitworks.step1.body:
We don't start by asking which ski area you want to go to. First we want to know who's coming. In a call of no more than 30 minutes we discuss how many colleagues are joining, how much skiing experience there is, whether there are non-skiers and what kind of group you are. We also cover the preferred period, trip length, transport, hotel level, activities and budget.
And we want to know why you're going in the first place: a reward after a good year, simply a few great days together, or should the trip also contribute to how people work together within the team? You don't need to write a detailed brief in advance. Half an hour of talking is enough to get us started.
howitworks.step2.title: We work out what fits
howitworks.step2.body:
After the call, we don't expect you to compare three hotels or research destinations yourself. We do that. We look at which of our ski areas best suit the group and then check what's actually available in your period.
We look at, among other things, hotels available for the whole group, the location relative to lifts and activities, transport, options for beginners and non-skiers, restaurants, activities, the level of comfort you're after and of course the budget. That takes a little more time than pulling a standard package from a catalogue. Expect around 2 to 3 working days.
howitworks.step3.title: You get a proposal
howitworks.step3.body:
We then come back with a concrete proposal. It sets out not only what we suggest, but also why we think it fits your group. That matters, because the person organising the trip is often not the one who approves the budget. HR may be enthusiastic while management or Finance still want to know what it costs, what you get for it, why this destination and what's included.
So we build the proposal so you can use it internally too. If there are two sensible options, we put them side by side: for example an ideal match and an alternative that's smarter on budget or availability.
howitworks.step4.title: Once approved, we arrange it
howitworks.step4.body:
This is the point where your internal organiser should actually get less work. Depending on the trip, we arrange things like transport (coach, flights, transfers), hotel and rooms, ski passes, ski rental, ski lessons, restaurants including reservations, and activities for both skiers and colleagues who want to do something else.
We put together a programme so everyone knows where to be and when, without every minute being fixed, and we handle participant communication so practical questions don't all land with one colleague. The goal is simple: the person who got the ski trip going shouldn't end up spending three months as its project manager.
howitworks.step5.title: We come along
howitworks.step5.body:
Bas and Carmen don't stay behind in the Netherlands or Belgium once the group has left. We support the trip on location. That means we're also there when the weather turns, someone can't find their gear, an activity has to change or something happens with a reservation at the last minute.
We can't prevent every problem. What we can do is make sure you don't have to solve it yourself.
howitworks.block1.title: How much do we arrange ourselves?
howitworks.block1.body:
A few things can only be done by you. We don't automatically know who's coming, who wants to share a room with whom, or which internal approvals are needed. For that we need information from you.
But as soon as we have that information, we pick up the legwork. We also try to communicate with participants directly about practical matters as much as possible, so questions don't have to travel down a long chain. If we can answer a question ourselves, we do.
howitworks.block2.title: Who communicates with the participants?
howitworks.block2.body:
We can handle the practical participant communication. Before departure we need to know, for example, who's skiing, who needs equipment, who wants lessons, whether there are dietary requirements and what information participants need. We gather and organise that directly as much as possible.
So you don't have to send a Teams message every few days asking everyone who still hasn't shared their ski boot size to please, really, do it today. That part can sit with us.
howitworks.block3.title: What if something changes after booking?
howitworks.block3.body:
Something almost always changes. Someone can no longer come, a new colleague does want to join, a room allocation shifts, a participant decides they want ski lessons after all, or a supplier changes something. On a group trip that's normal.
Pass the change on to us and we'll look at what's possible and what the effect on planning or cost might be. You don't have to start calling the hotel, ski school and rental company yourself.
howitworks.block4.title: And if something changes during the trip?
howitworks.block4.body:
Then we're there. We support the trip on location, so we're also around when the weather turns, someone can't find their gear, an activity has to change or something happens with a reservation at the last minute.
We can't prevent every problem. What we can do is make sure you don't have to solve it yourself.
howitworks.block5.title: How does the budget work?
howitworks.block5.body:
With us, a company ski trip has no fixed package price. The trips simply differ too much: a few days in Mayrhofen with a straightforward hotel is financially something very different from a luxury trip to Gstaad for a large group.
That's why we discuss budget during the intake. Not to see how much we can spend at most, but mainly to avoid working for two days on a trip that sounds wonderful but would never get approved. Based on your budget, we look for the best combination of destination, accommodation, transport and programme.
howitworks.block6.title: What's included in the price?
howitworks.block6.body:
In the proposal we make clear what's part of the trip. Depending on your choices, that can include transport, accommodation, breakfast, dinners, ski passes, ski rental, lessons, activities, local transport and our organisation and on-site support.
If certain elements aren't included or depend on final numbers, we say so. No surprises because three necessary items were still missing at the bottom of a quote.
howitworks.block7.title: How does payment work?
howitworks.block7.body:
Once approved, we lock in the reservations. The proposal and the agreement clearly state which payment moments apply and when we need final participant numbers.
Does the number of participants change after that? Then we let you know in advance what the financial consequences are, before we make any change.
howitworks.block8.title: When should we start organising?
howitworks.block8.body:
Better too early than too late. For a single hotel room there's usually still something to find. For 30 colleagues you might need 15 to 20 rooms, in the same hotel and in the same period. On top of that come restaurants, transport, lessons and activities.
The earlier we start, the more choice we have. That doesn't mean a trip at shorter notice is impossible. We just have to work with what's still available.
howitworks.block9.title: What do you need from us to start?
howitworks.block9.body:
Not much. We don't need a final room allocation, participant list or flight schedule yet. For the first call, a few things are enough: an indication of the number of participants, a preferred period or possible dates, an idea of the budget, roughly what kind of trip you have in mind, and 30 minutes to tell us about your team.
We work out the rest together.
howitworks.block10.title: Ready to see what's possible?
howitworks.block10.body:
You don't need to know yet whether you want Mayrhofen, Sölden, St. Anton, Kitzbühel, Zell am See-Kaprun or Gstaad. In fact, we'd rather work that out after we've spoken to you.
Tell us about your team for 30 minutes. Then we get to work.

about.b1.title: From the first conversation to the last descent
about.b1.body: With us, you don't first speak to someone in sales only to be handed off to three other people. Carmen and Bas are involved in the preparation and come along on the trip too. Above all, that means the person solving something during the trip knows exactly what was agreed beforehand. If a restaurant changes, someone turns out to need a ski lesson, or the programme has to shift because of the weather, you don't have to start calling and arranging things yourself. We do that.
about.b2.title: Why we go to the areas ourselves
about.b2.body: We could of course put together a list of hotels from the Netherlands or Belgium and build a nice programme around it. But then we still wouldn't know what it's really like. That's why we go to the areas we work with ourselves. We ski there, view the hotels, try out the activities and talk to local partners. Sometimes that turns up a fantastic hotel, sometimes a restaurant we'd never take a group to. And sometimes we discover that a hotel five minutes away is a far better choice than the pricier one right next to the lift. You won't spot that kind of thing on Google Maps.
about.b3.title: A limited number of trips per season
about.b3.body: During a company ski trip, we want to be there ourselves. That automatically means we can't send twenty groups to the Alps every weekend. And we don't want to. We'd rather work with a limited number of groups and stay involved in the trip ourselves than take on as many bookings as possible and then leave the delivery to someone else. So when a request comes in, we don't just look at whether a hotel is still available somewhere, but also at whether we can organise the trip the way we want to.

destinations.subtitle: The best destination doesn't exist. The one that fits your team best does.

destinations.grid.title: Six areas, six completely different company trips
destinations.grid.body: That's why we don't choose on piste kilometres or the best-known village alone. We look at ski experience, beginners, non-skiers, après-ski, calm, luxury, group size, timing and budget. Out of that comes an entirely different conversation.
destinations.solden.description: Sporty and always in motion, with the highest snow certainty of all our destinations thanks to the glacier.
destinations.mayrhofen.description: Energetic and lively. There's a dedicated programme here for non-skiers too, and the Hintertux glacier is open year-round.
destinations.stanton.description: A serious reputation, serious pistes, and the place where you know exactly which hotels are worth your money.
destinations.kitzbuhel.description: Well-known, polished and precisely for that reason deceptive: we know which restaurants can actually handle a group of twenty.
destinations.zellamsee.description: Quieter than it looks on paper. December and early spring are when this area works best for a group.
destinations.gstaad.description: Stylish and quiet, a tier above the rest. Not just because it's expensive, but because this is where the raclette hike is.

solden.signature.label: The moment that stays with you
solden.signature.title: Dinner at 3,048 metres, looking out over three countries
solden.signature.body: At the top of the Gaislachkogl there's a restaurant we ate at ourselves before proposing it to a group, not because it's famous from a film, but because at that altitude you're seated at the table while the clouds drift by below. No standard programme matches that.
solden.signature.caption: Gaislachkogl · 3,048 metres
mayrhofen.signature.label: The moment that stays with you
mayrhofen.signature.title: On the glacier in June. It's entirely possible.
mayrhofen.signature.body: The Hintertux Glacier is Austria's only year-round ski area, twenty minutes from Mayrhofen. We were still standing on the ice cave there in June, with a group around us. Not by chance, but as an option for anyone wanting to organise something outside the usual season, or simply to show that this exists.
mayrhofen.signature.caption: Hintertux · 3,250 metres
stanton.signature.label: The moment that stays with you
stanton.signature.title: Arlberg carries its own weight.
stanton.signature.body: The name Arlberg means something, even to someone who rarely skis. That makes a trip to St. Anton a different conversation from the start than 'we're going skiing'. We have made contact with Die Arlbergerin, a hotel with a story of its own in the village, which opens up a side of St. Anton you won't find simply by booking a room.
stanton.signature.caption: St. Anton am Arlberg · 1,304 m
kitzbuhel.signature.label: The moment that stays with you
kitzbuhel.signature.title: Kitzbühel is a name that sells itself.
kitzbuhel.signature.body: That is both its greatest strength and its pitfall. The well-known streets and facades of Kitzbühel are a statement, but the detail lies in Kirchberg and in the local knowledge we have built up. That gives access to the Kitzbühel behind the brand name, not just the street everyone already knows.
kitzbuhel.signature.caption: Kitzbühel · Tirol
zellamsee.signature.label: The moment that stays with you
zellamsee.signature.title: The lake makes the difference.
zellamsee.signature.body: At most ski destinations you look up into the mountain. Here you also look down into the valley, over the lake, with a view that on a clear day reaches across the Hohe Tauern. We have access here to corners of the valley that aren't in the standard brochure, including spots on the mountain that, for a group dinner, make the difference between an ordinary evening out and something that stays with you.
zellamsee.signature.caption: Zell am See · Salzburgerland
gstaad.signature.label: The moment that stays with you
gstaad.signature.title: The raclette walk.
gstaad.signature.body: You collect a raclette kit yourself from a little shop in the village, walk up the mountain to a hut that appears in no brochure, and light the fire yourself. Nobody arranges it for you. No guide, no group activity, no programme. That is exactly why it works, and why people are still talking about it months later.
gstaad.signature.caption: Saanenmöser · Switzerland
